title: Riyadh Airport Closure Extended as Saudi Arabia Tracks New Drone, Missile Threats
excerpt: Saudi civil aviation extended the King Khalid International Airport suspension with no reopening date, as the coalition tracked a fresh drone and cruise missile threat and probed how the weekend strikes got through.
body:
• Saudi Arabia extended the suspension of operations at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport on Monday, with no reopening date announced; one report put the closure through October 17.
  • The Saudi-led coalition said it had detected and was tracking a fresh drone and cruise missile threat, hours after air defences intercepted a ballistic missile aimed at Khamis Mushait.
  • The weekend attacks on the airport killed at least 14 people and wounded more than 320; authorities have opened a probe into how drones and missiles penetrated the capital's air defences.
  • If you are booked through Riyadh: Air France-KLM has suspended Riyadh flights through October 31 and Lufthansa through October 16, and Indian carriers have cancelled Saudi services through October 15 — check your airline before travelling.

Saudi Arabia extended the closure of Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport on Monday as its forces tracked a fresh drone and cruise missile threat, deepening the aviation shutdown that has emptied the skies over the Saudi capital since the weekend's deadly strikes.

The General Authority of Civil Aviation said the suspension would remain in place while inspections verify the safety and operational readiness of the airport's facilities. The authority gave no reopening date; Mint reported the closure would run through October 17. The extension came as Major General Turki Al-Malki, spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's government, said a threat involving drones and cruise missiles against the kingdom had been detected and was being dealt with. Earlier on Monday, Saudi air defences intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched toward Khamis Mushait in the southwest, and civil defence issued — then lifted — a potential-attack alert for Abha.

Three days of strikes

The airport has been attacked repeatedly since Saturday, when a strike on a departure terminal killed at least a dozen people and wounded more than 300. On Sunday an unidentified projectile struck Terminal 4, starting a fire that killed one man and injured 11 others — by one count the fourth strike on the airport in five days. The Houthis claimed responsibility for Saturday's attack and said they had also struck King Fahd International Airport in Dammam and two Saudi Aramco facilities. Our earlier coverage tracked the renewed strike on the airport and the allied travel warnings, and the Indian embassy's stay-indoors advisory for nationals in the kingdom.

How did the missiles get through?

Saudi authorities have opened an investigation into the air defence failure. Two regional officials told AP that an initial probe indicates the Houthis first fired multiple drones to pave the way for a mix of cruise and ballistic missiles, some of which can manoeuvre to evade Patriot interceptors. The probe is also examining why there was no earlier warning of weapons that travelled more than 1,000 kilometres to reach Riyadh. Aviation analytics firm Cirium recorded 99.7% of the airport's scheduled flights cancelled on Sunday.

What travellers face now

The disruption is widening beyond Saudi carriers. Air France and KLM have suspended Riyadh flights through October 31, Lufthansa Group's cancellations run through October 16, and the US Federal Aviation Administration has advised American carriers to exercise caution over Saudi Arabia while the EU's safety agency widened its airspace warning. Indian airlines have cancelled Saudi services through October 15. Iran, the Houthis' longtime backer, offered on Monday to mediate between the rebels and the kingdom. For the large Indian workforce in Saudi Arabia and travellers booked through Riyadh, the practical position is unchanged and worth repeating: the airport is closed, no reopening date is confirmed, and itineraries should be rechecked with the airline before any trip to the airport.
